ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A modern mass spectrometer can be used to analyze ions much heavier than protons; its schematic diagram is shown in the figure, in which the accelerating voltage is constant. A proton starts from rest at the entrance and is accelerated by the accelerating electric field, and after being deflected by a uniform magnetic field, leaves the magnetic field from the exit. If a certain singly charged positive ion starts from rest at the entrance and is accelerated by the same accelerating electric field, in order for it still to leave the magnetic field from the same exit after being deflected by the uniform magnetic field, the magnetic induction intensity needs to be increased to 12 times the original. The mass ratio of this ion to the proton is approximately

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A modern mass spectrometer can be used to analyze ions much heavier than protons; its schematic diagram is shown in the figure, in which the accelerating voltage is constant. A proton starts from rest at the entrance and is accelerated by the accelerating electric field, and after being deflected by a uniform magnetic field, leaves the magnetic field from the exit. If a certain singly charged positive ion starts from rest at the entrance and is accelerated by the same accelerating electric field, in order for it still to leave the magnetic field from the same exit after being deflected by the uniform magnetic field, the magnetic induction intensity needs to be increased to 12 times the original. Approximately what is the mass ratio of this ion to the proton?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The left side of the figure is marked “accelerating electric field,” with two vertical electrode plates and an arrow pointing to the right drawn, indicating that the positively charged particle is first accelerated from rest from the entrance in the electric field and enters the right-side region to the right. The right-side region is marked “magnetic field,” and a series of black dots are used to indicate a uniform magnetic field; after the particle enters the magnetic field, it is deflected along a dashed semicircular trajectory, and finally leaves the magnetic field from the “exit” marked on the left side. Therefore, for the proton and the unknown ion, if both leave from the same exit, what the figure corresponds to is that the orbital radii in the magnetic field are the same. Reasoning: The particle starts from rest and is accelerated through the same accelerating voltage U, satisfying qU = (1/2)mv^2. After entering the uniform magnetic field, it undergoes circular motion, with radius r = mv/(qB). Eliminating the velocity: v = sqrt(2qU/m), so r = m/(qB) * sqrt(2qU/m) = sqrt(2mU/q)/B. The unknown ion is a singly charged positive ion, with charge q = e, the same as the proton; the accelerating voltage U is the same; and because it still leaves from the same exit, the radius r is the same. Therefore B is proportional to sqrt(m), that is, B'/B = sqrt(m'/m_p). The problem gives B' = 12B, so 12 = sqrt(m'/m_p), obtaining m'/m_p = 12^2 = 144.
